title: Good Practice: Naming, Interlocks, Fail-Safe Design and Safety Limits
oneLiner: Habits that make PLC programs safe to run and easy to fix: clear names and comments, one place per output, interlocks, fail-safe wiring and defaults, testing, and why safety functions belong in safety-rated hardware, not a standard program.
keyTakeaway: Name signals for what they mean, write each output once, interlock anything that must never happen together, make every failure land safe, and never rely on a standard PLC program for a function that protects people: that needs a safety relay or safety PLC.
explanation:
Code that works is only the start. PLC programs run machines for decades and get read by an electrician in the middle of the night with the line stopped, so they need to be obvious. That means names that say what a signal is (Tank1_HighLevel, not I_0_3), comments that say why, each output written in exactly one place, sequences written as state machines, and the physical I/O mapped to named variables in one spot so a rewired sensor touches one line.

Interlocks and fail-safe design come next. An interlock is a condition that must be true before something may happen, such as a reverse contactor that can't close while forward is on. Fail-safe design means choosing, for every signal and output, what happens when a wire breaks or power is lost, and making that outcome safe: stop buttons wired normally closed, motors that stop when their output turns off, analog signals checked for wire break, and nothing that restarts by itself when power returns or a fault is reset.

Finally, there is a line a standard PLC must not cross. Emergency stops, guard interlocks, light curtains and two-hand controls protect people, and those functions are built with safety-rated equipment (a safety relay or a safety PLC) designed to the machinery safety standards, so they still work when the ordinary control system fails. The Safety & Redundancy lesson covers the fail-safe idea in general; this one shows where your program's responsibility ends.
